# AxioDB — Complete Documentation

Version: 20.3.1 | License: MIT | Node.js >= 20.0.0
npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/axiodb
GitHub: https://github.com/nexoral/AxioDB
Docs: https://axiodb.in

This file documents the actual, source-verified API surface of AxioDB — every method signature, every query/update/aggregation operator, and every constructor option that exists in the shipped code. Where an example below differs from what you may have seen elsewhere (including AxioDB's own README), this file is the corrected version; specific corrections are called out inline.

---

## What is AxioDB?

AxioDB is an embedded NoSQL database for Node.js with MongoDB-style queries. It is a pure JavaScript alternative to SQLite with zero native dependencies, no compilation step, and no platform-specific binaries. It works everywhere Node.js runs — Electron apps, CLI tools, local-first applications, and Node.js backends.

**One-liner:** `npm install axiodb` and you have a database. No mongod process, no node-gyp, no electron-rebuild.

**Sweet spot:** 10,000–500,000 documents per collection, documents of ~1 KB or larger, single process, with reads dominated by `documentId` lookups or indexed exact matches. See "Where AxioDB is the right choice" for why each of those three dimensions matters.

**Not a fit for:** 10M+ documents, multi-user web apps with hundreds of concurrent connections, relational data with JOINs, distributed/replicated/sharded systems, or cross-collection ACID transactions (AxioDB's transactions are scoped to a single collection).

---

## Services, Ports & Where Each One Lives

AxioDB is one package with several distinct surfaces. They are **not interchangeable**, and they are **not all distributed the same way**. Getting this wrong is the single most common mistake made when describing AxioDB.

| Service | What it is | Available in npm package? | Available in Docker image? | How to enable | Port |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Core embedded library** | The database itself, running in your process | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | `new AxioDB()` | none |
| **Dashboard (Web GUI)** | Browser UI to browse/edit data, with login + roles | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes (on by default) | `new AxioDB({ GUI: true })` / `AXIODB_GUI=true` | **27018** |
| **Dashboard HTTP API** | REST API behind that GUI (41 endpoints) | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | comes with the Dashboard; `HTTP: false` disables it | **27018** |
| **AxioDBCloud TCP server** | Lets other processes/machines use this database | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes (on by default) | `new AxioDB({ TCP: true })` / `AXIODB_TCP=true` | **27019** |
| **AxioDBCloud client** | Connects to that TCP server, same API as embedded | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | `const { AxioDBCloud } = require('axiodb')` | — |
| **CLI (Go)** | Command line interface — TCP queries, REPL, export/import via HTTP | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | `axiodb` binary | — |
| **MCP server (43 tools)** | Lets an AI agent operate the database | ❌ **NO** | ✅ Yes | `AXIODB_MCP=true` | **27020** |

**The MCP server is Docker-only.** It lives in `Docker/` in the repository, which is listed in `.npmignore`. Running `npm install axiodb` does **not** give you an MCP server. The only supported way to run it is the `theankansaha/axiodb` Docker image with `AXIODB_MCP=true`.

**Nothing here is a hosted/cloud service.** "AxioDBCloud" is the name of AxioDB's own TCP protocol and client — it is not a SaaS product, there is no account to sign up for, and Nexoral hosts no database for you. Every port above is on whatever machine or container *you* run AxioDB on. `https://axiodb.in` serves documentation only.

**Port summary:** `27018` = Dashboard + its HTTP API (HTTP). `27019` = AxioDBCloud TCP (custom binary-framed protocol, **not** HTTP). `27020` = MCP server (Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`, Docker only). 27018 and 27019 are hard-coded and not env-configurable — remap at the Docker layer (`-p host:container`). Only the MCP port is configurable, via `AXIODB_MCP_PORT`.

**Shared authentication:** the Dashboard, AxioDBCloud (when `TCPAuth: true`), and the MCP server all read the same user/role store in the reserved `config` database. One `admin` account, one forced-password-change, one lockout policy across all three.

---

## Installation

```bash
npm install axiodb
```

Requires Node.js >= 20.0.0, npm >= 6.0.0. Server-side/desktop only — does not run in a browser (needs the filesystem).

---

## Quick Start

```javascript
const { AxioDB } = require('axiodb');

const db = new AxioDB({ GUI: true }); // GUI at http://localhost:27018

const myDB = await db.createDB('HelloWorldDB');
const collection = await myDB.createCollection('greetings');

await collection.insert({ message: 'Hello, Developer!' });

const result = await collection.query({}).exec();
console.log(result.data.documents[0].message); // Hello, Developer!
```

`AxioDB` is a hard singleton — only one instance per process. Constructing a second one throws `Only one instance of AxioDB is allowed.`

---

## AxioDB (root instance)

```typescript
new AxioDB(options?: {
  GUI?: boolean;          // Enable web GUI + HTTP API on port 27018 (default: false)
  HTTP?: boolean;         // Enable HTTP API server on port 27018 (default: true when GUI is on; GUI: true + HTTP: false throws error)
  RootName?: string;      // Root storage folder name (default: "AxioDB")
  CustomPath?: string;    // Custom storage path (default: current working directory)
  TCP?: boolean;          // Enable AxioDBCloud TCP server on port 27019 (default: false)
  TCPAuth?: boolean;      // Require username/password on TCP connections, same RBAC as GUI (default: false)
  TLS?: boolean;          // Encrypt the TCP server with TLS (default: false)
  TLSCertPath?: string;   // Path to a PEM cert file - required if TLS: true
  TLSKeyPath?: string;    // Path to the matching PEM private key - required if TLS: true
})
```

If `GUI: true` and `HTTP: false`, the constructor throws — the GUI needs the HTTP server to serve its UI. If `GUI: false` and `HTTP: true`, only the REST API runs on port 27018 (no UI — the browser shows "GUI is disabled").

If `TLS: true` but either path is missing/unreadable, the constructor throws immediately — it never silently falls back to plaintext.

```typescript
db.createDB(dbName: string): Promise<Database>
db.deleteDatabase(dbName: string): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
db.isDatabaseExists(dbName: string): Promise<boolean>
db.getInstanceInfo(): Promise<SuccessInterface | undefined>
```

There is no schema-validation parameter on `createDB` or `createCollection` — AxioDB is schema-less. (If you've seen a `createDB(name, schemaValidation)` or `createCollection(name, enc, key, schema)` signature anywhere, that's not a real feature.)

---

## Database

```typescript
database.createCollection(
  name: string,
): Promise<Collection>

database.deleteCollection(name: string): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
database.isCollectionExists(name: string): Promise<boolean>
database.getCollectionInfo(): Promise<SuccessInterface | undefined>
```

---

## Collection

```typescript
collection.insert(document: object): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
collection.insertMany(documents: object[] | object): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
collection.query(query: object): Reader
collection.update(query: object): UpdateOperation
collection.delete(query: object): DeleteOperation
collection.aggregate(pipeline: object[]): Aggregation
collection.newIndex(...fieldNames: string[]): Promise<SuccessInterface>
collection.dropIndex(indexName: string): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
collection.getIndexes(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
collection.totalDocuments(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
collection.beginTransaction(): Transaction
collection.startSession(options?: SessionOptions): Session
collection.findByIds(ids: string[]): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
```

`query()`, `update()`, `delete()`, and `aggregate()` all return chainable objects — nothing happens until you call the terminal method (`.exec()`, `.UpdateOne()`, `.deleteMany()`, etc.). There is no `collection.findAll()` method.

`insert()` is routed through a single-operation transaction internally, so it is Write-Ahead-Log-backed: if the process crashes mid-write, the next collection open (`Transaction.recoverTransactions()`, run automatically on `Collection` construction) redoes or undoes the half-finished write from the WAL.

### Insert

```javascript
await users.insert({ name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com', age: 30 });

await users.insertMany([
  { name: 'Bob', age: 25 },
  { name: 'Carol', age: 35 },
]);
```

`documentId` and `updatedAt` are set automatically — don't set them yourself, they'll be overwritten.

---

## Query (Reader)

```typescript
collection.query(query: object): Reader

reader.Limit(n: number): Reader
reader.Skip(n: number): Reader
reader.Sort(sort: object): Reader            // { field: 1 } ascending, { field: -1 } descending
reader.setCount(count: boolean): Reader      // include totalDocuments in the result
reader.setProject(fields: object): Reader    // { field: 1 } to include only that field
reader.findOne(matchOneOnly?: boolean): Reader  // still needs .exec() after - see below
reader.exec(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
reader.hint(fieldName: string): Reader    // force use of a specific index
```

`findOne()` returns `Reader` for chaining, not a Promise directly — you must still call `.exec()`:

```javascript
const one = await users.query({ email: 'alice@example.com' }).findOne(true).exec();
```

```javascript
const all = await users.query({}).exec();

const paginated = await users
  .query({ role: 'admin' })
  .Sort({ age: -1 })
  .Limit(10)
  .Skip(20)
  .setProject({ name: 1, email: 1 })
  .exec();

const withCount = await users.query({ role: 'admin' }).setCount(true).exec();
```

### Index hints

Force the query engine to use a specific index instead of scanning:

```javascript
// Without hint: might scan the full collection
// With hint: forces use of the 'status' index
const active = await users.query({ status: 'active' }).hint('status').exec();
```

Index hints are useful when the query planner picks a suboptimal index, or when you want to guarantee a specific index is used for performance-critical queries.

### Query operators (full list)

These work on any field passed to `.query()` — this is the complete set as implemented, more than what's usually documented:

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `$gt` | Greater than | `{ age: { $gt: 25 } }` |
| `$gte` | Greater than or equal | `{ age: { $gte: 18 } }` |
| `$lt` | Less than | `{ age: { $lt: 60 } }` |
| `$lte` | Less than or equal | `{ price: { $lte: 100 } }` |
| `$eq` | Equal | `{ status: { $eq: 'active' } }` |
| `$ne` | Not equal | `{ status: { $ne: 'inactive' } }` |
| `$in` | Value in array | `{ role: { $in: ['admin', 'mod'] } }` |
| `$nin` | Value not in array | `{ tag: { $nin: ['spam'] } }` |
| `$exists` | Field present/absent | `{ email: { $exists: true } }` |
| `$regex` | Regular expression (use `$options` for flags, default `'i'`) | `{ name: { $regex: '^John', $options: 'i' } }` or a real `RegExp` |
| `$not` | Negates a nested condition | `{ age: { $not: { $lt: 18 } } }` |
| `$type` | Value's JS type (`'string'`, `'number'`, `'array'`, `'null'`, ...) | `{ age: { $type: 'number' } }` |
| `$size` | Array length equals | `{ tags: { $size: 3 } }` |
| `$all` | Array contains every given value | `{ tags: { $all: ['a', 'b'] } }` |
| `$elemMatch` | At least one array element matches a nested query | `{ items: { $elemMatch: { qty: { $gt: 5 } } } }` |
| `$or` | Logical OR (top-level) | `{ $or: [{ age: { $lt: 18 } }, { age: { $gt: 65 } }] }` |
| `$and` | Logical AND (top-level) | `{ $and: [{ age: { $gt: 18 } }, { active: true }] }` |
| `$nor` | None of the given conditions match (top-level) | `{ $nor: [{ status: 'banned' }, { status: 'deleted' }] }` |

`$gt`/`$gte`/`$lt`/`$lte` can be combined on the same field (e.g. a range query `{ age: { $gte: 18, $lte: 65 } }`). `documentId` and single-field exact-match queries on an indexed field use the index for O(1) lookup; everything else falls back to a full collection scan.

---

## Update

```typescript
collection.update(query: object): UpdateOperation

updater.Sort(sort: object): UpdateOperation
updater.UpdateOne(data: object): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>   // first match only
updater.UpdateMany(data: object): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface> // every match
```

```javascript
await users.update({ name: 'Alice' }).UpdateOne({ role: 'superadmin' });
await users.update({ role: 'trial' }).UpdateMany({ role: 'active' });
```

**Important correction:** updates are a **flat merge** — `data` is shallow-merged onto the existing document (`{ ...oldDoc, ...data }`). There is no MongoDB-style update-operator support (`$inc`, `$set`, `$push`, `$pull`, `$unset`, etc.). If you write `.UpdateOne({ $inc: { balance: -100 } })`, it does **not** increment `balance` — it literally sets a field named `"$inc"` to `{ balance: -100 }` on the document. To increment a value, read it and write the new value yourself:

```javascript
const doc = await users.query({ name: 'Alice' }).exec();
const newBalance = doc.data.documents[0].balance - 100;
await users.update({ name: 'Alice' }).UpdateOne({ balance: newBalance });
```

Updating a document only touches the index entries for fields whose value actually changed (not every indexed field on the document), so unrelated indexed fields keep their existing order.

---

## Delete

```typescript
collection.delete(query: object): DeleteOperation

deleter.Sort(sort: object): DeleteOperation
deleter.deleteOne(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>   // first match only
deleter.deleteMany(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface> // every match
```

```javascript
await users.delete({ name: 'Dave' }).deleteOne();
await users.delete({ active: false }).deleteMany();
```

---

## Batch Read (findByIds)

Retrieve multiple documents by their IDs in a single call:

```typescript
collection.findByIds(ids: string[]): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
```

```javascript
const docs = await users.findByIds(['doc1', 'doc2', 'doc3']);
console.log(docs.data.documents); // array of matching documents
```

Missing IDs are silently omitted from the result — no error is thrown for non-existent IDs.

---

## Aggregation

```typescript
collection.aggregate(pipeline: object[]): Aggregation

aggregation.exec(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
```

```javascript
const stats = await users.aggregate([
  { $match: { active: true } },
  { $group: { _id: '$role', count: { $sum: 1 }, avgAge: { $avg: '$age' } } },
  { $sort: { count: -1 } },
  { $project: { role: 1, count: 1 } },
  { $limit: 10 },
]).exec();
```

```javascript
// Cross-collection join with $lookup
const usersWithOrders = await users.aggregate([
  { $lookup: {
      from: 'Orders',
      localField: 'userId',
      foreignField: 'userId',
      as: 'userOrders'
  }},
  { $unwind: '$userOrders' },
  { $match: { 'userOrders.status': 'completed' } },
  { $group: { _id: '$name', totalSpent: { $sum: '$userOrders.total' } } }
]).exec();
```

```javascript
// Custom operator registration
import { OperatorRegistry } from 'axiodb';

OperatorRegistry.registerAccumulator('$median', (collection, expr) => {
  const values = collection.map(doc => doc[expr.field]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const mid = Math.floor(values.length / 2);
  return values.length % 2 ? values[mid] : (values[mid - 1] + values[mid]) / 2;
});
```

`$match` is no longer required as the first stage — the engine scans the entire pipeline for a `$match` and uses it for index optimization regardless of position.

Supported stages:

- **`$match`** — filters documents. Supports exact equality, `RegExp`, `$regex`/`$options`, `$gte`, `$gt`, `$lte`, `$lt`, `$ne`, `$in`, `$nin`, `$exists`, `$not`, `$elemMatch`, `$all`, `$size`, `$type`, `$mod`, and top-level logical operators `$and`, `$or`, `$nor`.
- **`$group`** — groups by `_id` (literal, `'$fieldName'`, or composite object). Accumulators: `$sum`, `$avg`, `$min`, `$max`, `$first`, `$last`, `$push`, `$addToSet`, `$stdDevPop`, `$stdDevSamp`.
- **`$sort`** — `{ field: 1 | -1, ... }`, multi-field support.
- **`$project`** — inclusion (`1`), exclusion (`0`), and computed fields via expressions (`{ bonus: { $multiply: ['$salary', 0.1] } }`).
- **`$limit`** — `{ $limit: n }`.
- **`$skip`** — `{ $skip: n }`.
- **`$unwind`** — string form `{ $unwind: '$field' }` or object form `{ $unwind: { path: '$field', includeArrayIndex: 'idx', preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true } }`.
- **`$addFields` / `$set`** — computed fields via expressions.
- **`$unset`** — remove fields.
- **`$lookup`** — cross-collection join. Equality form: `{ from, localField, foreignField, as }`. Pipeline form: `{ from, let, pipeline, as }`. Uses index optimization on foreign collection when indexes exist.
- **`$facet`** — multi-facet aggregation with parallel sub-pipelines.
- **`$bucket` / `$bucketAuto`** — bucket documents by boundaries or automatic distribution.
- **`$count`** — count documents.
- **`$sortByCount`** — group by expression, sort by count descending.
- **`$sample`** — random sample of N documents.
- **`$replaceRoot` / `$replaceWith`** — replace document with subdocument.

Expression evaluator supports 80+ operators across arithmetic, string, comparison, logical, array, date, type, and set categories. Custom operators can be registered via `OperatorRegistry.registerStageOperator()`, `registerAccumulator()`, and `registerExpressionOperator()`.

---

## Transactions

Transactions are ACID and scoped to a single collection, with savepoints, rollback, and Write-Ahead Logging for crash recovery.

```typescript
collection.beginTransaction(): Transaction

transaction.insert(data: object): Transaction               // chainable, queues the op
transaction.update(query: object, data: object): Transaction
transaction.delete(query: object): Transaction
transaction.savepoint(name: string): Transaction
transaction.rollbackTo(name: string): Transaction
transaction.releaseSavepoint(name: string): Transaction
transaction.commit(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
transaction.rollback(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
```

Same flat-merge caveat as regular `Update`: `transaction.update(query, data)` shallow-merges `data` onto the existing document — no `$inc`/`$set` operators here either.

```javascript
const tx = collection.beginTransaction();
try {
  tx.insert({ name: 'Charlie', balance: 500 });
  tx.savepoint('checkpoint1');
  tx.update({ name: 'Alice' }, { active: false });
  const result = await tx.commit();
} catch (err) {
  await tx.rollback();
}
```

`commit()`'s success payload includes `documentIds: string[]` — the documentId(s) of any `insert()` operations in that transaction.

---

## Session

MongoDB-like session wrapper around `Transaction`, adding automatic retry.

```typescript
collection.startSession(options?: {
  defaultTimeout?: number;  // ms, default 60000
  retryWrites?: boolean;    // default true
  maxRetries?: number;      // default 3
}): Session

session.getSessionId(): string
session.isSessionActive(): boolean
session.startTransaction(): Transaction   // only one active transaction per session at a time
session.withTransaction(callback: (txn: Transaction) => Promise<void>): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
session.commitTransaction(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
session.abortTransaction(): Promise<SuccessInterface | ErrorInterface>
session.endSession(): Promise<void>
```

```javascript
const session = collection.startSession();
await session.withTransaction(async (tx) => {
  tx.insert({ name: 'Alice', balance: 1000 });
  tx.update({ name: 'Bob' }, { active: true });
  // Auto-commits on success, auto-rolls-back on error
});
```

`withTransaction` automatically retries (exponential backoff, up to `maxRetries`) when the failure looks transient — its message contains `timeout`, `lock`, `deadlock`, `conflict`, `busy`, `temporary`, `EBUSY`, or `EAGAIN` (case-insensitive). Anything else fails immediately, no retry.

---

## Indexing

```javascript
await users.newIndex('email');                  // single field
await users.newIndex('email', 'age', 'role');    // multiple fields, one call
await users.dropIndex('email');
await users.getIndexes();
```

`documentId` is always indexed automatically — no setup needed, O(1) lookups. Every index is dual-written (in-memory cache + disk); the in-memory copy has a randomized 5–15 minute TTL (staggered on purpose, to avoid a cache-stampede when many entries would otherwise expire at once) and reloads from disk on a cold start or cache miss. A query that isn't an indexed exact match, or whose index misses, falls back to a full collection scan.

---

## Built-in Web GUI & RBAC

```javascript
const db = new AxioDB({ GUI: true }); // http://localhost:27018
```

Features: visual database/collection browser, real-time data inspection, query execution UI, performance monitoring, index management API (`GET /api/index/list`, `POST /api/index/create`, `DELETE /api/index/delete`).

On first start (`GUI: true` or `TCP: true` + `TCPAuth: true`), AxioDB seeds a reserved `config` database (hidden from the normal database list, and blocked from being read/written directly — `403 "This is a reserved system database"`) with a default account:

```
Username: admin
Password: admin
```

Forced password change on first login, for every account, not just the default one — no way around it other than completing it via the GUI. Predefined roles:

| Role | Access |
|------|--------|
| Super Admin | Full access, including user/role management |
| Admin | Full database/collection/document access, no user/role management |
| View | Read-only |

Login rate limiting: 5 failed attempts from one IP within a trailing 15-minute window → 15-minute lockout (`429`), shared between the GUI and TCP `AUTHENTICATE`. Sessions live only in server memory (never persisted) — restarting the server logs everyone out.

---

## AxioDBCloud — Remote TCP Access

Same API as embedded AxioDB, over a TCP connection. The wire protocol has exactly **32 commands** (`source/tcp/types/command.types.ts`):

`PING`, `HEALTH`, `DISCONNECT`, `AUTHENTICATE`, `CREATE_DB`, `DELETE_DB`, `DB_EXISTS`, `GET_INSTANCE_INFO`, `CREATE_COLLECTION`, `DELETE_COLLECTION`, `COLLECTION_EXISTS`, `GET_COLLECTION_INFO`, `INSERT_DOCUMENT`, `INSERT_MANY_DOCUMENTS`, `QUERY_DOCUMENTS`, `QUERY_BY_ID`, `UPDATE_DOCUMENT_BY_ID`, `UPDATE_DOCUMENTS_BY_QUERY`, `DELETE_DOCUMENT_BY_ID`, `DELETE_DOCUMENTS_BY_QUERY`, `AGGREGATE`, `TOTAL_DOCUMENTS`, `CREATE_INDEX`, `DROP_INDEX`, `LIST_INDEXES`, `BEGIN_TRANSACTION`, `COMMIT_TRANSACTION`, `ROLLBACK_TRANSACTION`, `SAVEPOINT`, `ROLLBACK_TO_SAVEPOINT`, `RELEASE_SAVEPOINT`, `FIND_BY_IDS`

You normally never send these by hand — the `AxioDBCloud` client wraps them behind the same `createDB`/`createCollection`/`query` API as the embedded library. `client.sendCommand()` is the escape hatch if you need one directly.

### Server

```javascript
const { AxioDB } = require('axiodb');
const db = new AxioDB({ TCP: true, RootName: 'MyDB', CustomPath: '.' });          // plaintext, no auth
const db = new AxioDB({ TCP: true, TCPAuth: true, RootName: 'MyDB', CustomPath: '.' }); // auth required, shares GUI's RBAC
const db = new AxioDB({ TCP: true, TLS: true, TLSCertPath: './cert.pem', TLSKeyPath: './key.pem' }); // TLS-encrypted
```

### Client

```typescript
new AxioDBCloud(connectionString: string, options?: {
  timeout?: number;              // request timeout, ms (default: 30000)
  reconnectAttempts?: number;    // default: 10
  reconnectDelay?: number;       // initial backoff, ms (default: 1000)
  heartbeatInterval?: number;    // PING/PONG interval, ms (default: 30000)
  username?: string;             // if server has TCPAuth: true
  password?: string;
  maxPoolSize?: number;          // concurrent pooled connections (default: 10, mirrors MongoDB driver option)
  tls?: boolean;                 // must match server's TLS setting
  tlsCAPath?: string;            // CA/self-signed cert to validate server against, when tls: true
  tlsRejectUnauthorized?: boolean; // default true - only disable for local/dev, never production
})

client.connect(): Promise<void>          // must be awaited before any other call
client.disconnect(): Promise<void>
client.login(username: string, password: string): Promise<AuthenticatedUser>
client.authenticatedUser: AuthenticatedUser | undefined   // getter
client.sendCommand(command: string, params: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>  // low-level escape hatch
client.createDB(name: string): Promise<DatabaseProxy>
client.deleteDatabase(name: string): Promise<void>
client.isDatabaseExists(name: string): Promise<boolean>
client.getInstanceInfo(): Promise<SuccessInterface | undefined>
client.getPinnedConnection(): PooledConnection | null  // for transaction pinning
```

### Transaction Proxy (TCP)

```typescript
collection.beginTransaction(): Promise<TransactionProxy>

transactionProxy.insert(data: object): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.insertMany(documents: object[]): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.findByIds(ids: string[]): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.query(query: object, options?): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.updateById(documentId: string, updateData: object): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.updateByQuery(query: object, updateData: object, updateOne?: boolean): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.deleteById(documentId: string): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.deleteByQuery(query: object, deleteOne?: boolean): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.savepoint(name: string): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.rollbackToSavepoint(name: string): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.releaseSavepoint(name: string): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.commit(): Promise<unknown>
transactionProxy.rollback(): Promise<unknown>
```

All operations on a TransactionProxy are pinned to a single TCP connection so in-flight writes are visible to subsequent reads within the same transaction. On disconnect, orphaned transactions are automatically rolled back server-side.
client.on('poolDegraded', (event: { requested, connected, failed, errors }) => {})
client.on('error', (err) => {})
```

```javascript
const { AxioDBCloud } = require('axiodb');

const client = new AxioDBCloud('axiodb://localhost:27019', { username: 'admin', password: 'admin' });
await client.connect(); // auto-authenticates since credentials were passed in the constructor

const db = await client.createDB('ProductionDB');
const users = await db.createCollection('Users');
await users.insert({ name: 'Alice' });
const results = await users.query({ role: 'admin' }).Limit(10).exec();

await client.disconnect();
```

`connect()` resolves even if the pool comes up smaller than `maxPoolSize` requested (emits `poolDegraded`) — as long as at least one pool member connected. If the very first connection fails, `connect()` rejects outright.

**DoS protections (server-side, not configurable at runtime):** max 1,000 total concurrent connections; max 100 concurrent connections per IP (`429`); max 300 connection attempts per IP per 10s, else 30s cooldown (`429`).

**TLS:** off by default, plaintext wire protocol otherwise. You must supply your own cert/key (AxioDB never generates one). Self-signed certs need `tlsCAPath` on the client to be trusted, or the client refuses to connect by default.

---

## Docker Deployment

```bash
docker run -d \
  --name axiodb-server \
  -p 27018:27018 -p 27019:27019 \
  -e AXIODB_TCP_AUTH_ENABLED=true \
  -v axiodb-data:/app \
  theankansaha/axiodb
```

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `AXIODB_GUI` | `true` | HTTP GUI on port 27018 |
| `AXIODB_HTTP` | mirrors GUI | HTTP API on port 27018 — auto-enables when GUI is on; `AXIODB_GUI=true` + `AXIODB_HTTP=false` is an error |
| `AXIODB_TCP` | `true` | AxioDBCloud TCP server on port 27019 |
| `AXIODB_TCP_AUTH_ENABLED` | `true` | Require TCP authentication (shared RBAC with GUI) |
| `AXIODB_TLS` | `false` | Encrypt TCP with TLS |
| `AXIODB_TLS_CERT_PATH` | *(none)* | In-container path to PEM cert — required if `AXIODB_TLS=true` |
| `AXIODB_TLS_KEY_PATH` | *(none)* | In-container path to PEM key — required if `AXIODB_TLS=true` |
| `AXIODB_ROOT_NAME` | `AxioDB` | Root storage folder name |
| `AXIODB_CUSTOM_PATH` | container's working dir | Storage path inside the container |
| `AXIODB_MCP` | `false` | Enable the MCP server on port 27020 |
| `AXIODB_MCP_PORT` | `27020` | MCP server port |

Ports (27018/27019) aren't env-configurable — remap at the Docker layer (`-p host:container`). TCP auth is **on by default** in the published image; complete the `admin`/`admin` forced password change via the GUI before connecting over TCP.

`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` matters under concurrent disk I/O — the published image auto-computes it from the container's actual CPU allotment (`4 × allotted CPUs`, clamped `[4, 64]`); override with `-e UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16` if needed.

---

## MCP Server — AI Agent Integration

**Availability: Docker image only.** The MCP server lives in the repository's `Docker/` directory, which is listed in `.npmignore`, so it is not published to npm. `npm install axiodb` gives you the database, not the MCP server. The only supported way to run it is the `theankansaha/axiodb` image with `AXIODB_MCP=true`.

```bash
docker run -d -e AXIODB_GUI=true -e AXIODB_MCP=true \
  -p 27018:27018 -p 27019:27019 -p 27020:27020 \
  -v axiodb-data:/app theankansaha/axiodb
```

43 tools at `http://localhost:27020/mcp` covering databases, collections, documents, aggregation, indexes, dashboard stats, health, transactions, and user/role management — gated by the same RBAC as the GUI (a View-role session gets a real `403` on write tools). Every tool except `axiodb_login` requires a `sessionId` from logging in first. Compatible with Claude Code, Codex CLI, opencode, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, and Google Antigravity — see https://axiodb.in/mcp-server for exact registration commands per tool.

---

## Troubleshooting

- **"Not connected to server" right after `connect()`:** `connect()` is async — always `await` it before using the client.
- **`401` Authentication required:** a command was sent before a successful `AUTHENTICATE`. Pass `{ username, password }` in the constructor, or call `client.login(...)` first.
- **`403` must change password before TCP use:** applies to every account on first use, including a freshly created one. Complete it via the GUI, then reconnect.
- **`429` too many failed logins:** 5 failures/IP/15min → 15-minute lockout, shared between GUI and TCP.
- **`429` too many concurrent connections:** per-IP cap is 100 concurrent sockets, independent of authentication.
- **`429` too many connection attempts:** per-IP churn guard, 300 attempts/10s → 30s cooldown.
- **`403` reserved system database:** the `config` database is AxioDB's own RBAC storage — use a different name.
- **Connection refused/timeout:** confirm `TCP: true` (or `AXIODB_TCP=true`) and the port is published/reachable; a protocol error mentioning "HTTP data on TCP port" usually means you're pointed at 27018 (GUI) instead of 27019 (TCP).
- **`EMFILE`/`ENFILE` at high concurrency:** each client opens `maxPoolSize` sockets; raise `ulimit -n` (bare-metal) or `--ulimit nofile=65536:65536` (Docker) — the published image already raises its own soft limit.

---

## Performance (10,000-document benchmark, illustrative — not a guarantee)

- Single insert: ~3ms · InsertMany (10 docs): ~87ms
- `documentId` lookup (indexed): ~1ms · `findOne`: ~1ms
- Query with `$gt`: ~469ms · Query with `$in`: ~401ms · Sort: ~382ms · Full scan: ~2.6s
- `UpdateOne`: ~8ms · `UpdateMany` (full collection): ~466ms
- `deleteOne`: ~3ms · `deleteMany`: ~446ms
- Transaction insert: ~23ms · Transaction update: ~14ms · Rollback: ~3ms

---

## Comparisons

### vs SQLite / better-sqlite3

| | SQLite / better-sqlite3 | AxioDB |
|---|---|---|
| Native dependencies | Yes (C bindings) | None |
| Query language | SQL strings | JS objects |
| Schema migrations | Required | Schema-less |
| Built-in caching | No | Yes |
| Multi-core | No | Worker Threads |
| Built-in GUI | No | Yes |
| Best for | 10M+ records, relational | 10K–500K docs, embedded |

### vs lowdb / nedb

| | lowdb | nedb | AxioDB |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maintained | Yes | No (abandoned) | Yes |
| Native bindings | None | None | None |
| Storage | Single JSON file | Single file/in-memory | File-per-document |
| Query language | JS/Lodash | JS objects | JS objects (MongoDB-style) |
| Built-in caching | No | No | Yes |
| Worker Threads | No | No | Yes |
| ACID transactions | No | No | Yes |
| TypeScript | Yes | Partial | Full |
| Sweet spot | <5K docs | <100K docs | 10K–500K docs |
| Built-in GUI | No | No | Yes |

### vs MongoDB

| | MongoDB | AxioDB |
|---|---|---|
| Server required | Yes | No — embedded |
| Network access | Yes | Optional (AxioDBCloud) |
| Scale | Distributed, unlimited | Single node, 10K–500K docs |
| Best for | Multi-user production | Desktop apps, CLI tools |

---

## Using AxioDB as a SQLite Alternative in Node.js

This is AxioDB's primary positioning: **the database you reach for when you wanted SQLite, but do not want a native module.**

### Why people replace SQLite/better-sqlite3 with AxioDB

`better-sqlite3` and `node-sqlite3` are C libraries with Node bindings. That means a compiled `.node` binary that must match the exact combination of OS, CPU architecture, and Node/Electron ABI version. In practice that produces:

- `node-gyp` builds failing on machines without Python/build tools
- `electron-rebuild` as a mandatory extra step, re-run on every Electron upgrade
- `NODE_MODULE_VERSION xx does not match yy` at runtime
- separate CI matrix builds per platform for prebuilt binaries
- Docker images that need `build-essential` just to `npm install`
- Alpine/musl vs glibc mismatches

AxioDB has **zero native dependencies**. It is plain JavaScript reading and writing files. `npm install axiodb` is the whole install on every platform, every Node version ≥ 20, and every Electron version. There is no build step, no rebuild step, no prebuilt-binary matrix, and no ABI to match.

### Concept mapping

| SQLite | AxioDB |
|---|---|
| Database file (`app.db`) | A directory tree under `RootName`/`CustomPath` |
| `TABLE` | Collection |
| Row | Document (a JSON object, one file per document) |
| Column | Field (no fixed set — schema-less) |
| `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` / `rowid` | `documentId` (auto-generated string, always indexed) |
| `CREATE TABLE` + migrations | `database.createCollection(name)` — no schema, no migrations |
| `CREATE INDEX` | `collection.newIndex('email')` |
| `BEGIN` / `COMMIT` / `ROLLBACK` | `collection.beginTransaction()` / `.commit()` / `.rollback()` |
| `SAVEPOINT` | `transaction.savepoint('name')` / `.rollbackTo('name')` |
| WAL mode | Always on — every write is WAL-backed, recovered on next open |
| SQL string | JavaScript object query |

### SQL → AxioDB cookbook

```javascript
// SELECT * FROM users
await users.query({}).exec();

// SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 25
await users.query({ age: { $gt: 25 } }).exec();

// SELECT * FROM users WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 65
await users.query({ age: { $gte: 18, $lte: 65 } }).exec();

// SELECT * FROM users WHERE role IN ('admin','mod')
await users.query({ role: { $in: ['admin', 'mod'] } }).exec();

// SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'John%'
await users.query({ name: { $regex: '^John', $options: 'i' } }).exec();

// SELECT name, email FROM users ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20
await users.query({})
  .Sort({ age: -1 }).Limit(10).Skip(20)
  .setProject({ name: 1, email: 1 })
  .exec();

// SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?     (fastest path — always indexed)
await users.query({ documentId: 'ABC123' }).exec();

// SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users
await users.totalDocuments();

// INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES ('Alice', 30)
await users.insert({ name: 'Alice', age: 30 });

// UPDATE users SET role='active' WHERE role='trial'
await users.update({ role: 'trial' }).UpdateMany({ role: 'active' });

// DELETE FROM users WHERE active = 0
await users.delete({ active: false }).deleteMany();

// SELECT role, COUNT(*), AVG(age) FROM users WHERE active=1 GROUP BY role
await users.aggregate([
  { $match: { active: true } },
  { $group: { _id: '$role', count: { $sum: 1 }, avgAge: { $avg: '$age' } } },
]).exec();
```

### What you give up by leaving SQLite

Be honest about these — they are real:

- **No JOINs and no foreign keys.** Denormalize, or do a second query in JavaScript.
- **No SQL.** Existing SQL, ORMs (Prisma, Drizzle, Knex, TypeORM, Sequelize), and SQL tooling do not work with AxioDB.
- **No `$inc`/`$set`-style update operators.** Updates are a flat shallow merge; read-modify-write for arithmetic.
- **Cross-collection transactions do not exist.** A transaction is scoped to one collection.
- **Lower ceiling.** SQLite is comfortable into the tens of millions of rows; AxioDB targets 10K–500K documents per collection.
- **Unindexed queries are a full scan.** Only `documentId` and single-field exact matches on an indexed field are O(1); a `$gt` scan over 10,000 documents is ~469ms, not ~1ms.
- **No standard file format.** A SQLite file opens in a hundred tools; AxioDB's tree does not.

### Stay on SQLite when

You need SQL or an ORM; you have genuinely relational data with JOINs; you are past ~1M rows; you need heavy analytical queries over large datasets; or you need to hand the database file to another program that speaks SQLite.

### Choose AxioDB when

Your install must never compile anything (Electron, CLI tools distributed with npx, serverless-ish images, locked-down CI); your data is document-shaped JSON; you want MongoDB-style queries without running MongoDB; you are inside the 10K–500K range; or you want a built-in admin GUI without building one.

---

## Electron & Embedded/Desktop Applications

Electron is AxioDB's primary target. The entire value proposition is that **there is no `electron-rebuild` step, ever** — no `.node` file to match against Electron's V8/ABI version, so upgrading Electron cannot break your database layer.

### Correct setup

Run AxioDB in the **main process** only. It needs filesystem access, and the singleton must live in exactly one process.

```javascript
// main.js (Electron main process)
const { app, ipcMain } = require('electron');
const path = require('path');
const { AxioDB } = require('axiodb');

// Store data in Electron's per-user data directory, NOT inside the app bundle
// (app.asar is read-only, and app directories get replaced on update).
const db = new AxioDB({
  RootName: 'AppData',
  CustomPath: app.getPath('userData'),
  GUI: false,           // keep the dashboard off in a shipped desktop app
});

let users;
app.whenReady().then(async () => {
  const appDB = await db.createDB('AppDB');
  users = await appDB.createCollection('users');
  await users.newIndex('email');
});

// Renderer talks to the database over IPC — never directly.
ipcMain.handle('users:find', async (_event, query) => {
  const result = await users.query(query).Limit(100).exec();
  return result.data.documents;
});
```

```javascript
// preload.js
const { contextBridge, ipcRenderer } = require('electron');
contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('db', {
  findUsers: (query) => ipcRenderer.invoke('users:find', query),
});
```

### Electron rules

- **Main process only.** Do not enable `nodeIntegration` to use AxioDB from a renderer. Use `ipcMain.handle` + `contextBridge`, as above.
- **`CustomPath: app.getPath('userData')`.** Never write inside the app directory or `app.asar` — asar is read-only and app contents are replaced on update, which would delete user data.
- **One instance.** `new AxioDB()` twice throws. Create it once in `main.js` and export/reuse it.
- **`GUI: false` in production.** The dashboard opens port 27018; a shipped desktop app should not listen on a port unless you intend it to.
- **Validate IPC input.** A renderer is untrusted input. Do not pass a raw renderer-supplied object straight into `.query()` if the renderer can be compromised.
- **No rebuild in packaging.** `electron-builder` / `electron-forge` need no special configuration for AxioDB — no `buildDependenciesFromSource`, no `npmRebuild`, no native-module unpacking rules.

Same reasoning applies to other embedded/desktop contexts: Tauri sidecars running Node, NW.js, VS Code extensions, CLI tools shipped via `npx`, Raspberry Pi / ARM boards (no cross-compilation), and container images that must stay free of build toolchains.

---

## Source Code Structure

Repository: https://github.com/nexoral/AxioDB. TypeScript in `source/`, compiled to CommonJS in `lib/`.

```
source/
├── config/
│   ├── DB.ts                       Entry point — exports AxioDB, AxioDBCloud, InstanceTypes
│   ├── Keys/Permissions.ts         RBAC permission catalogue, session cookie name, rate-limit constants
│   └── Interfaces/                 Shared TypeScript interfaces
├── Services/                       Core database engine
│   ├── Indexation.operation.ts     The AxioDB singleton; starts the Dashboard and/or TCP server
│   ├── Database/                   createCollection, deleteCollection, collection registry
│   ├── Collection/                 insert, query, update, delete, aggregate, index, transaction entry points
│   ├── CRUD Operation/             Create / Reader / Update / Delete operations
│   ├── Index/Index.service.ts      Index storage (JSONL, append-only) + metadata
│   ├── Aggregation/                Pipeline engine, 60+ stages, $lookup, expression evaluator, OperatorRegistry
│   ├── Transaction/                Transaction, Session, WAL, LockManager, TransactionRegistry
│   └── Auth/                       SessionStore (memory-only), LoginRateLimiter, RBAC checks
├── engine/Filesystem/              FileManager, FolderManager — all low-level disk I/O
├── Memory/memory.operation.ts      InMemoryCache, randomized 5–15 minute TTL per entry
├── utility/Searcher.utils.ts       Query operator evaluation ($gt, $in, $regex, $elemMatch, ...)
├── Helper/                         Converter, Response builders
├── server/                         Dashboard + HTTP API (Fastify, port 27018)
│   ├── router/                     Route definitions
│   ├── controller/                 Auth, Database, Collection, Index, Operation controllers
│   └── middleware/auth.middleware.ts   Session cookie + permission enforcement
├── tcp/                            AxioDBCloud TCP server (port 27019)
│   ├── types/command.types.ts      The 32-command CommandType enum
│   ├── handler/CommandHandler.ts   Command dispatch
│   └── handler/handlers/           Auth, DB, Collection, Operation handlers
└── client/                         AxioDBCloud client + Database/Collection proxies

Docker/                             NOT published to npm (.npmignore)
├── Dockerfile                      EXPOSE 27018 27019 27020
├── runner.js                       Reads AXIODB_* env vars, boots the instance
├── mcpServer.js                    MCP server, Streamable HTTP on port 27020 at /mcp
└── mcp/tools/                      The 43 MCP tools, one file per feature area

Test/modules/                       crud, transaction, read, auth, tcp-auth, tcp-noauth,
                                    tcp-transaction, tcp-tls, crash-recovery, mcp-confirm
Document/                           This documentation site (React + Vite, deployed to axiodb.in)
```

### On-disk layout

```
{CustomPath}/{RootName}/
└── {DatabaseName}/
    ├── collection.meta.jsonl            collection registry (append-only)
    └── {CollectionName}/
        ├── {documentId}.axiodb          one file per document
        ├── indexes/
        │   ├── index.meta.jsonl         index registry (append-only)
        │   └── {fieldName}.jsonl        one JSONL index file per indexed field
        └── .transactions/
            ├── txn-meta.jsonl           in-flight transaction registry (append-only)
            └── {transactionId}.wal.jsonl  write-ahead log, one per transaction
```

Documents are the only thing on disk that is not JSONL. Every registry and log is append-only, one JSON object per line: adding an entry is an O(1) append rather than a read-parse-rewrite of the whole file, and reading streams line by line instead of loading the file whole. The registries fold to their current state on read (last line wins per key) and are truncated once nothing is left to track.

WAL files use `.wal.jsonl` rather than a bare `.jsonl` because crash recovery scans `.transactions/` by suffix — a bare `.jsonl` would match `txn-meta.jsonl` and replay the registry as if it were a transaction's log.

One file per document is what makes `documentId` lookups O(1) — the path is computed, not searched. It is also what sets the sweet spot, and it has two costs worth knowing before you choose AxioDB.

### The cost of one file per document

**Disk usage is dominated by the filesystem block size, not by your data.** A filesystem allocates whole blocks — 4 KB on ext4, APFS and NTFS — so a 128-byte document still occupies 4 KB. Measured on ext4:

| Documents | Logical size | Actual on disk | Amplification |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20,000 × ~130 B | 2.6 MB | 80 MB | **31×** |

The amplification is `4096 / your_document_size`, so it disappears as documents grow: a 4 KB document wastes nothing, a 500-byte document wastes 8×, a 128-byte document wastes 32×. **If you store many small records, budget roughly 4 KB each regardless of their real size.** At the top of the supported range — 500K small documents — that is about 2 GB on disk for perhaps 64 MB of actual data.

**Full scans pay one syscall trio per document.** A query that is not a `documentId` lookup or an indexed exact match reads every document in the collection, which means one `open`/`read`/`close` per file rather than a single sequential read. Measured on the same 20,000 documents:

| Operation | File-per-document | Equivalent single JSONL file |
|---|---|---|
| Write 20,000 documents | 780 ms | 85 ms (**9× faster**) |
| Full scan of 20,000 documents | 208 ms | 20 ms (**10× faster**) |

(Warm page cache, consumer SSD, single-threaded. Cold cache or spinning disks widen the gap; the disk-usage figure is exact either way.)

**What the design buys in return**, and why it is not simply a worse choice: `documentId` lookups are O(1) with no index consulted, a torn write damages exactly one document rather than a shared file, deletes are `unlink` and updates are an atomic rename — so there are no tombstones and no compaction pass to schedule, and nothing to go wrong during one.

**Practical guidance:** if your documents are small (< 1 KB) and you expect hundreds of thousands of them, or your workload is dominated by unindexed scans rather than key lookups, index the fields you filter on — or use SQLite or PostgreSQL, which pack rows into shared pages and were built for that shape.

### Where AxioDB is the right choice

The same design that costs you space on tiny documents is what makes it excellent inside its range. AxioDB is at its best when all three of these hold:

| Dimension | Ideal | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Document size** | **~1 KB and above** | At 4 KB and up there is zero space overhead — the block is full either way. A 4 KB document stores in 4 KB, exactly like a row in a page-based engine, with none of the page-cache machinery. |
| **Collection size** | **10K–500K documents** | Enough that a flat JSON file is unusable, not so many that per-file syscalls and directory size dominate. |
| **Access pattern** | **`documentId` lookups and indexed exact matches** | The path is computed, so a read is one `open` — no B-tree descent, no query planner, no index page reads. This is the case where AxioDB is genuinely *faster* than a page-based engine, not merely adequate. |

Add the deployment constraint that nothing else solves: **your install must never compile anything.** Electron apps, CLI tools shipped via `npx`, locked-down CI, minimal container images. `better-sqlite3` cannot do this — it ships compiled C that must match your OS, CPU architecture and Node/Electron ABI. That is the one thing AxioDB does that SQLite cannot, and it is usually the reason to pick it.

**The profile it was built for:** an Electron or CLI app storing tens of thousands of records of a kilobyte or more — user documents, notes, sync state, cached API payloads, event records — read mostly by id or by an indexed field, in a single process, where shipping a native module is unacceptable. In that shape AxioDB is not a compromise against SQLite; it is the better fit.

**The profile to send elsewhere:** millions of rows, documents of a few hundred bytes each, analytical scans over whole collections, several processes sharing one dataset, JOINs, or anything needing an ORM.

---

## The 43 MCP Tools (Docker only)

Available **only** via the Docker image with `AXIODB_MCP=true`, at `http://localhost:27020/mcp` (Streamable HTTP). Every tool except `axiodb_login` requires a `sessionId` returned by `axiodb_login`. Destructive tools additionally prompt the human through the MCP client before running.

- **Auth (4):** `axiodb_login`, `axiodb_logout`, `axiodb_whoami`, `axiodb_change_own_password`
- **Database (4):** `axiodb_create_database`, `axiodb_delete_database`, `axiodb_database_exists`, `axiodb_get_instance_info`
- **Collection (4):** `axiodb_create_collection`, `axiodb_delete_collection`, `axiodb_collection_exists`, `axiodb_get_collection_info`
- **Document (8):** `axiodb_insert_document`, `axiodb_insert_many_documents`, `axiodb_query_documents`, `axiodb_update_document`, `axiodb_delete_document`, `axiodb_aggregate`, `axiodb_total_documents`, `axiodb_find_documents_by_ids`
- **Index (3):** `axiodb_create_index`, `axiodb_drop_index`, `axiodb_list_indexes`
- **Dashboard (2):** `axiodb_health`, `axiodb_get_dashboard_stats`
- **User (5):** `axiodb_create_user`, `axiodb_delete_user`, `axiodb_list_users`, `axiodb_update_user_role`, `axiodb_reset_user_password`
- **Role (4):** `axiodb_create_role`, `axiodb_delete_role`, `axiodb_list_roles`, `axiodb_list_permissions`
- **Transactions (9):** `axiodb_begin_transaction`, `axiodb_transaction_insert`, `axiodb_transaction_update`, `axiodb_transaction_delete`, `axiodb_transaction_savepoint`, `axiodb_transaction_rollback_to_savepoint`, `axiodb_transaction_release_savepoint`, `axiodb_commit_transaction`, `axiodb_rollback_transaction`

---

## Limitations

### Hard boundaries (not tunable)

| Boundary | Value | Where enforced |
|---|---|---|
| AxioDB instances per process | **1** — a second `new AxioDB()` throws | `Indexation.operation.ts` |
| Transaction scope | single collection — no cross-collection ACID | `Services/Transaction/` |
| Total concurrent TCP connections | **1,000** | `tcp/config/keys.ts` |
| Concurrent TCP connections per IP | **100** → `429` | `tcp/config/keys.ts` |
| TCP connection attempts per IP | **300 per 10s** → 30s cooldown | `tcp/config/keys.ts` |
| Failed logins per IP | **5 per 15 min** → 15-minute lockout | `config/Keys/Permissions.ts` |
| Dashboard port | **27018**, not configurable | remap via Docker `-p` |
| TCP port | **27019**, not configurable | remap via Docker `-p` |
| MCP port | 27020, configurable via `AXIODB_MCP_PORT` | Docker only |
| Node.js | **>= 20.0.0** | `package.json` engines |

### Design limits

- **Scale:** optimized for 10K–500K documents per collection. Beyond ~1M, migrate to PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or SQLite.
- **Disk usage per document:** one file per document means each one occupies at least one filesystem block (typically 4 KB), whatever its real size. 20,000 documents of ~130 bytes measured at 80 MB on disk against 2.6 MB of data — 31× amplification. Budget ~4 KB per document for small records. See "The cost of one file per document" above.
- **Concurrency:** single-instance, single-node. Fine for a desktop app or a modest service; not for hundreds of concurrent web users.
- **No JOINs, no foreign keys, no referential integrity.** Denormalize or join in JavaScript.
- **No replication, sharding, or clustering.** One node, one copy. Back it up yourself.
- **No MongoDB update operators.** `$inc`, `$set`, `$push`, `$pull`, `$unset` do not exist — update data is a flat shallow merge.
- **`$lookup` loads the entire foreign collection into memory.** No streaming join — large foreign collections can cause memory pressure.
- **Unindexed queries are full scans.** Only `documentId` and single-field exact matches on an indexed field are O(1).
- **No browser support.** Node.js and a real filesystem are required.
- **Sessions are memory-only.** Restarting the server logs every Dashboard/TCP user out.
- **Sorting/filtering happens in memory** after the candidate set is read — memory use scales with result size, not with the collection.
- **The `config` database name is reserved** for AxioDB's own RBAC storage (`403` if you try to use it).

None of this is a shortcoming to apologize for — it's a deliberately scoped embedded/local-first niche. Outgrowing it is a sign to migrate, not a bug.

---

## FAQ

**Is AxioDB a MongoDB replacement?** No — AxioDB is embedded (runs inside your app), MongoDB is client-server. Use AxioDB for desktop/CLI/local-first up to ~500K documents.

**Does it work with Electron?** Yes, it's the primary use case — zero native deps means no electron-rebuild, no `.node` files.

**Does update support `$inc`/`$set`/other MongoDB update operators?** No. Update data is a flat, shallow merge onto the existing document. See the Update section above.

**How many documents can it handle?** Optimized for 10K–500K. Use PostgreSQL/MongoDB for 1M+.

**TypeScript support?** Full, built-in — no separate `@types` package.

**Browser support?** No — Node.js (v20+) and filesystem access only.

**What is AxioDBCloud?** AxioDB's own TCP protocol and client on port 27019, with the exact same API as embedded AxioDB — up to 1,000 concurrent connections, auto-reconnect, optional TLS and shared-RBAC authentication. It is **not** a hosted service: you run the server, there is no account, and Nexoral stores none of your data.

**Is AxioDB a drop-in replacement for SQLite?** Not drop-in — the query language is different (JavaScript objects, not SQL) and there are no JOINs. But it is a direct replacement in the sense that matters most for Node.js and Electron: same embedded, single-file-tree, no-server model, without any native module. See the "Using AxioDB as a SQLite Alternative" section for a full SQL→AxioDB cookbook.

**Do I need node-gyp, a compiler, or electron-rebuild?** No. There is no native code at all, so nothing compiles and nothing can mismatch your Node/Electron ABI.

**Is the MCP server included in `npm install axiodb`?** No. It is Docker-image-only (`theankansaha/axiodb` with `AXIODB_MCP=true`, port 27020). This is the single most commonly mis-stated fact about AxioDB.

**Which ports does AxioDB open?** None by default. 27018 with `GUI: true` (Dashboard + HTTP API). 27019 with `TCP: true` (AxioDBCloud). 27020 in Docker with `AXIODB_MCP=true` (MCP). 27018/27019 are fixed in code — remap with Docker `-p`.

**Can two parts of my app each create an AxioDB instance?** No — `new AxioDB()` twice in one process throws. Create it once and export it.

**Are transactions cross-collection?** No. A transaction is scoped to a single collection.

**Where is my data stored?** `{CustomPath}/{RootName}/{Database}/{Collection}/`, one `.axiodb` file per document, plus an `indexes/` folder of `.jsonl` index files and a `.transactions/` folder holding the transaction registry and write-ahead logs. Documents are the only non-JSONL files on disk.
